items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Oaxaca, Mexico, told in the second person.

You wake before the roosters because your grandmother is already grinding corn. You help her carry the baskets to the market, past the church and the bakery where Don Félix waves with floury hands.
You speak Zapotec with her and Spanish with the customers and English with the tourists who ask to take your photo.
By noon you are three people. On the bus home, your grandmother falls asleep on your shoulder, and you are only one: hers.

Identify the device in the quotation "You wake before the roosters".
items.answer: second-person narration
items.markingKey: B. "You wake before the roosters" is an example of second-person narration: it makes the reader experience the routine as if it were their own.

items.stem: Distinguish between physical setting and cultural setting.
items.answer: Physical setting is the place and time (a Seoul street at 11 p.m.); cultural setting is the values, customs and expectations of the community (academic pressure, family honour).
items.markingKey: Physical setting is the place and time (a Seoul street at 11 p.m.); cultural setting is the values, customs and expectations of the community (academic pressure, family honour). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Stories from other cultures are only about differences." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They often explore universal experiences – family, pressure, belonging – in a specific cultural context.
items.markingKey: They often explore universal experiences – family, pressure, belonging – in a specific cultural context. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Lagos.

When the rains came, Mama said the city became honest. 'Lagos cannot hide her potholes under water,' she said, 'and people cannot hide their hearts under umbrellas.'
That evening the road outside our compound turned into a brown river. Mr Adeyemi from next door, who had not spoken to us since the argument about the generator, waded across carrying a sack of rice above his head.
'Your roof is leaking,' he said. 'Mine is not. Come.'
We spent the night in his parlour, two families, one candle, nobody mentioning the generator.

Explain how the cultural setting shapes the story.
items.answer: Cultural setting: a Lagos compound in the rainy season, with shared generators, neighbours who know each other's business, and community hospitality in a crisis.
items.markingKey: Cultural setting: a Lagos compound in the rainy season, with shared generators, neighbours who know each other's business, and community hospitality in a crisis. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify two details that reveal cultural values in the Seoul story and explain what each suggests.
items.answer: Hagwon until 11 p.m. – the importance of education; the university car sticker – status and family comparison.
items.markingKey: Hagwon until 11 p.m. – the importance of education; the university car sticker – status and family comparison.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Readers need to share a culture to fully understand a story set in it."
items.answer: Insiders may notice more, but well-written stories allow outsiders to understand and empathise; reading across cultures broadens perspective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: insiders recognise subtle details and values; outsiders may misread. Arguments against: good stories communicate universal emotions; outsiders can learn and empathise. Supported judgement: Insiders may notice more, but well-written stories allow outsiders to understand and empathise; reading across cultures broadens perspective.

items.answer: The customs, beliefs, language and daily life of the community in which a story is set

Read the following extract from a short story set in Oaxaca, Mexico, told in the second person.

You wake before the roosters because your grandmother is already grinding corn. You help her carry the baskets to the market, past the church and the bakery where Don Félix waves with floury hands.
You speak Zapotec with her and Spanish with the customers and English with the tourists who ask to take your photo.

How does the writer use second-person narration to explore identity?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: Second-person narration makes the reader live the narrator's day. The list of three languages shows her shifting between identities, and the metaphor "By noon you are three people" captures the strain of switching. The ending contrasts this with "you are only one: hers", suggesting that her truest identity lies in her family and Zapotec heritage.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Second-person narration makes the reader live the narrator's day. The ending contrasts this with "you are only one: hers", suggesting that her truest identity lies in her family and Zapotec heritage. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a contemporary novel about a refugee student in Berlin.

On the first day, the teacher wrote my name on the board wrong. Nobody corrected her, so I didn't either.
Now, six months later, everyone calls me Sami instead of Samir, and I answer to it like a dog answers to a whistle.
In history we studied walls – the Berlin Wall, how it divided families. Lena put up her hand and said, "At least that's all in the past."
I thought of my uncle, still on the other side of a border, still waiting. I didn't put up my hand.

Explain how the narrative perspective shapes what the reader knows and feels.
items.answer: First-person narration reveals Samir's private thoughts that classmates never hear, creating dramatic irony when Lena says divisions are "in the past".
items.markingKey: First-person narration reveals Samir's private thoughts that classmates never hear, creating dramatic irony when Lena says divisions are "in the past". Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Alabama in 1955.

The bus was crowded and hot. Ruth sat in the middle section with her mother, behind the painted line, where coloured passengers were allowed to sit if no white passenger needed the seat.
At the third stop a man got on. There was nowhere for him to sit.
The driver looked in the mirror. "Y'all better make it light on yourselves," he said.
Ruth felt her mother's hand tighten on hers. Three people stood up. Her mother did not.
Ruth had never heard silence so loud.

What impression does the reader get of the main character? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Ruth's mother is quietly courageous: she stays seated despite the threat. Ruth is a child observer who senses danger through her mother's tightening hand and the "loud" silence.
items.markingKey: Ruth's mother is quietly courageous: she stays seated despite the threat. Ruth is a child observer who senses danger through her mother's tightening hand and the "loud" silence. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

At 11 p.m. the hagwon let us out. The street was bright as noon with study cafés and convenience stores. My mother was waiting in the car with a kimbap roll and the question she asks every night: "How did you do?"

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a Gothic short story.

Blackwater Hall had been empty for forty years, yet every night a candle burned in the highest window.
I arrived in November, when the trees had given up their leaves and the fog lay on the moor like a shroud. The gates groaned open before I touched them.
Inside, the air was colder than the night. Portraits lined the staircase – generations of pale Blackwaters – and every pair of painted eyes was turned, I swear, towards the door.
Towards me.

Why might the writer have chosen this narrative voice? Refer to the text.
items.answer: First-person narration ("I swear") makes the reader share the narrator's fear, but the insistence "I swear" also hints that the narrator expects not to be believed.
items.markingKey: First-person narration ("I swear") makes the reader share the narrator's fear, but the insistence "I swear" also hints that the narrator expects not to be believed. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Explain how one detail in the extract connects to a wider theme.
items.answer: Theme: kindness and moral choice. How it is developed: Repetition ("Every morning he told himself...") establishes his avoidance, so the shift "Then, on Thursday" signals change. Short, parallel sentences ("The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward.") slow the pace as he weighs his options, and the detail of the "empty purse" raises the stakes. The whispered ending resolves the tension with kindness while leaving his motives ambiguous.

items.stem: "Stories from other cultures are only about differences." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They often explore universal experiences – family, pressure, belonging – in a specific cultural context.

items.answer: In fiction, second person can create intimacy and immediacy, placing the reader inside the character's experience.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Soweto, South Africa, in 1976.

The new rule came on a Monday: half our subjects would now be taught in Afrikaans. Mathematics. Geography. A language most of our teachers barely spoke.
Thabo tore the notice from the classroom door. "They want to teach us in the language of the people who made the pass laws," he said.
I said nothing. I was fourteen and I wanted to pass my exams.
By June I was marching beside him, holding a cardboard sign: WE ARE NOT AFRAID. My hands were shaking so much the letters blurred.

Explain what the character's actions and words reveal about them.
items.answer: The narrator changes from cautious and self-focused ("I wanted to pass my exams") to politically active, though still frightened (shaking hands). Thabo is defiant and outspoken.
items.markingKey: The narrator changes from cautious and self-focused ("I wanted to pass my exams") to politically active, though still frightened (shaking hands). Thabo is defiant and outspoken. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Seoul.

At 11 p.m. the hagwon let us out. The street was bright as noon with study cafés and convenience stores. My mother was waiting in the car with a kimbap roll and the question she asks every night: "How did you do?"
"Ninety-two," I said.
She smiled, but I saw her eyes go to the number on Ji-woo's mother's car sticker: SEOUL NATIONAL UNIVERSITY.
I ate the kimbap. It tasted of seaweed and expectation.

Identify the technique used in "the number on Ji-woo's mother's car sticker: SEOUL NATIONAL UNIVERSITY" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Symbol: "the number on Ji-woo's mother's car sticker: SEOUL NATIONAL UNIVERSITY" – the sticker symbolises status and comparison between families.
items.markingKey: Symbol: "the number on Ji-woo's mother's car sticker: SEOUL NATIONAL UNIVERSITY" – the sticker symbolises status and comparison between families. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a Gothic short story.

Blackwater Hall had been empty for forty years, yet every night a candle burned in the highest window.
I arrived in November, when the trees had given up their leaves and the fog lay on the moor like a shroud. The gates groaned open before I touched them.
Inside, the air was colder than the night. Portraits lined the staircase – generations of pale Blackwaters – and every pair of painted eyes was turned, I swear, towards the door.
Towards me.

Identify the point of view from which this extract is told and explain its effect.
items.answer: First-person narration ("I swear") makes the reader share the narrator's fear, but the insistence "I swear" also hints that the narrator expects not to be believed.
items.markingKey: First-person narration ("I swear") makes the reader share the narrator's fear, but the insistence "I swear" also hints that the narrator expects not to be believed. How does the writer present the pressure on the narrator?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The cultural setting – hagwon finishing at 11 p.m., a street "bright as noon" – shows study dominating life. The mother's nightly question and her glance at the university sticker reveal comparison, interpreted silently by the first-person narrator. The final line "It tasted of seaweed and expectation" turns even a caring act (bringing food) into a reminder of pressure.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "First-person narration is the best choice for stories about identity."
items.answer: First person is powerful for identity, but second and third person offer other insights; the best choice depends on what the story explores.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inner thoughts reveal identity; the voice expresses culture and language. Arguments against: second person can involve readers more; third person can show how others see the character. Supported judgement: First person is powerful for identity, but second and third person offer other insights; the best choice depends on what the story explores. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.
